claim: The early Drosophila embryo has been an important system for studying epithelial morphogenesis.
source: The early Drosophila embryo has been an important system for studying epithelial morphogenesis (Blankenship et al., 2006; Kiehart et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2009), as it is readily amenable to genetic techniques, high-resolution imaging, and physical perturbations.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Ventral furrow formation is an early morphogenetic event in which the mesoderm moves from the exterior to the interior of the fly embryo.
source: Ventral furrow formation, an early morphogenetic event in which the mesoderm moves from the exterior to the interior of the fly embryo, has been particularly widely studied process which is understood in great genetic and molecular detail (Ko and Martin, 2020; Stathopoulos and Newcomb, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Studies on the physical mechanisms of ventral furrow formation have failed to reach a consensus regarding what spatiotemporal patterns of mechanical forces and material properties drive this physical transformation.
source: The physical mechanisms by which the ventral furrow forms have also been widely examined, but these studies have failed to reach a consensus regarding what spatiotemporal patterns of mechanical forces and material properties drive this physical transformation (Fierling et al., 2022; Heer et al., 2017; Perez-Mockus et al., 2017; Polyakov et al., 2014; Rauzi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A truly predictive mechanical model of ventral furrow formation would require an accurate representation of the patterns of forces and the patterns of material properties in the embryo.
source: A truly predictive mechanical model of ventral furrow formation would require an accurate representation of the patterns of forces and the patterns of material properties in the embryo, since these two factors combined determine the dynamics of tissue movement.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about mechanical modeling requirements

claim: Optical and magnetic tweezers typically generate forces in the piconewton range.
source: Optical and magnetic tweezers (Bambardekar et al., 2015; Tanase et al., 2007) typically generate forces in the piconewton range, such that the resulting displacements do not exceed a few microns.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Forces from optical and magnetic tweezers are usually applied on a time-scale of seconds.
source: Additionally, those forces are usually applied on a time-scale of seconds.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature in the preceding sentence

claim: Morphogenesis typically unfolds on a time-scale of tens of minutes or hours and results in deformations on the order of tens to hundreds of microns.
source: Hence, the force- and time-scales in these measurements tend to be well below the scales characteristic of morphogenesis, which typically unfolds on a time-scale of tens of minutes or hours and results in deformations on the order of tens to hundreds of microns.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of morphogenetic processes

claim: Material properties are expected to vary depending on the time- and force-scales involved.
source: Since material properties are in general expected to vary depending on the time- and force-scales involved, such measurements may not be relevant for understanding the physical mechanisms underlying morphogenesis.
evidence: Based on established principles of material science

claim: Bendable cantilevers and biological atomic force microscopes allow for applying much larger forces over larger times than optical and magnetic tweezers.
source: Bendable cantilevers and biological atomic force microscopes (AFM) allow for applying much larger forces over larger times (Fernández and Ott, 2008; Fischer-Friedrich et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Cantilevers and AFM techniques are hard to use in living embryos since introducing a probe into an embryo without significantly disrupting the tissue proves challenging.
source: However, these techniques are hard to use in living embryos since introducing a probe into an embryo without significantly disrupting the tissue proves challenging.
evidence: Based on practical considerations of experimental technique

claim: Ferrofluid droplet-based measurement techniques allow probing tissue with forces on the order of tens of nanonewtons.
source: Recently, we and one other lab introduced a measurement technique based on the use of ferrofluid droplets (Doubrovinski et al., 2017; Serwane et al., 2017). This method allows probing tissue with forces on the order of tens of nanonewtons, but requires a probe that is fairly large (10–20 µm; several-fold larger than a typical cell), thus possibly locally damaging the tissue that is being probed.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Ferrofluid droplet probes are fairly large (10–20 µm; several-fold larger than a typical cell), thus possibly locally damaging the tissue that is being probed.
source: This method allows probing tissue with forces on the order of tens of nanonewtons, but requires a probe that is fairly large (10–20 µm; several-fold larger than a typical cell), thus possibly locally damaging the tissue that is being probed.
evidence: Based on inference from probe size relative to cell size

claim: The viscosity of cytoplasm in the Drosophila embryo is approximately 1000 cP.
source: Previously, we and others used ferrofluid droplets to measure the viscosity of cytoplasm in the Drosophila embryo, which we found to be approximately 1000 cP (Doubrovinski et al., 2017; Selvaggi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cited publications

claim: Elasticity in the Drosophila embryo is largely due to F-actin.
source: We also demonstrated that elasticity is largely due to F-actin, indicating that the actin-rich cortex is the primary source of elasticity, and we quantified the time-scale of elastic stress relaxation (Doubrovinski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cited publication

claim: The actin-rich cortex is the primary source of elasticity in the Drosophila embryo.
source: We also demonstrated that elasticity is largely due to F-actin, indicating that the actin-rich cortex is the primary source of elasticity, and we quantified the time-scale of elastic stress relaxation (Doubrovinski et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that elasticity is due to F-actin, which is enriched in the cortex

claim: Response to applied force in the Drosophila embryo is dominated by elastic forces and geometric constraints.
source: By analyzing data from a series of experiments in which embryonic epithelium is subjected to developmentally relevant perturbations, we conclude that the response to applied force is adiabatic and is dominated by elastic forces and geometric constraints, or system size effects.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and computational modeling presented in the manuscript

claim: The apical surface of the epithelium must be softer than the basal surface.
source: Crucially, computational modeling of the experimental data indicated that the apical surface of the epithelium must be softer than the basal surface, a result which we confirmed experimentally.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental validation

claim: Different compartments of the same cell can have very different mechanical properties.
source: Specifically, different compartments of the same cell can have very different mechanical properties; when they do, they can contribute differently to different mechanical stimuli and cannot be merely averaged together.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and computational modeling presented in the manuscript

claim: Tissue geometry can play a substantial role in mechanical response.
source: Additionally, tissue geometry can play a substantial role in mechanical response, and cannot be neglected.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: A standard injection glass pipette is used as a mold for making a PDMS cantilever.
source: Briefly, a standard injection glass pipette is used as a mold for making a PDMS (polydimethylsiloxane) cantilever.
evidence: Description of the experimental method

claim: The tip of a glass pipette is filled with an uncured mixture of polymer, crosslinker, and a green variant of BODIPY dye.
source: The tip of a glass pipette is filled with an uncured mixture of polymer, crosslinker, and a green variant of BODIPY (boron-dipyrromethene) dye, which enters by capillary action through an opening at the tip.
evidence: Description of the experimental method

claim: After the polymer is cured, the tip of the glass scaffold is etched away in a solution of hydrofluoric acid to expose the soft PDMS core.
source: After the polymer is cured, the tip of the glass scaffold is etched away in a solution of hydrofluoric acid to expose the soft PDMS core.
evidence: Description of the experimental method

claim: During cellularization, membranes extend from the surface of the embryo and protrude between the nuclei, such that the cytoplasm is for the first time partitioned into individual cells.
source: Subsequently, in the process of cellularization, membranes extend from the surface of the embryo and protrude between the nuclei, such that the cytoplasm is for the first time partitioned into individual cells (Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: During cellularization, every newly forming cell is in effect open on its basal side, such that the interior of that cell is connected to the yolk compartment residing in the center of the embryo.
source: During cellularization, every newly forming cell is in effect open on its basal side, such that the interior of that cell is connected to the yolk compartment residing in the center of the embryo (see Figure 1b for a schematic illustration).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1b

claim: When a fly embryo is cut along one side, the side that is not cut continues to develop completely normally showing no noticeable defects.
source: Importantly, we found that when a fly embryo is cut along one side, the side that is not cut continues to develop completely normally showing no noticeable defects.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The cantilever is translated at a constant velocity of 0.5 µm/s for approximately 60 s during the loading phase.
source: First, during the loading phase, the base of the cantilever is translated at a constant velocity of 0.5 µm/s for approximately 60 s.
evidence: Description of the experimental protocol

claim: During the holding phase, the cantilever is held in place for approximately 60 s.
source: Next, during the holding phase, the cantilever is held in place for approximately 60 s.
evidence: Description of the experimental protocol

claim: In the unloading phase, the cantilever is rapidly retracted from the interior of the cell, and the cellular layer is then allowed to freely relax.
source: Finally, in the unloading (or relaxation) phase, the cantilever is rapidly retracted from the interior of the cell, and the cellular layer is then allowed to freely relax.
evidence: Description of the experimental protocol

claim: Cantilever deflection is linearly proportional to the force being applied to it for the range of deflections observed.
source: This can be done because cantilever deflection is linearly proportional to the force being applied to it for the range of deflections observed.
evidence: Based on established principles of material mechanics

claim: The Young's modulus of the PDMS comprising the cantilever was estimated to be 1.6 MPa by measuring deformation of a macroscopic rod under its own weight.
source: The three methods estimate the Young's modulus of the PDMS comprising the cantilever to be 1.6 MPa, 0.9±0.17 MPa, and 2.1±0.23 MPa, respectively (the first value is based on a single measurement, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurement shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b

claim: The Young's modulus of the PDMS comprising the cantilever was estimated to be 0.9±0.17 MPa by pulling the cantilever through a fluid of known viscosity.
source: The three methods estimate the Young's modulus of the PDMS comprising the cantilever to be 1.6 MPa, 0.9±0.17 MPa, and 2.1±0.23 MPa, respectively
evidence: Supported by experimental measurement shown in Figure 3a-b

claim: The Young's modulus of the PDMS comprising the cantilever was estimated to be 2.1±0.23 MPa by probing the cantilever with an AFM probe.
source: The three methods estimate the Young's modulus of the PDMS comprising the cantilever to be 1.6 MPa, 0.9±0.17 MPa, and 2.1±0.23 MPa, respectively
evidence: Supported by experimental measurement shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c-d

claim: The average force measured at maximal tissue displacement (at the end of the loading phase) was 11.1±1.2 nN.
source: The average force measured at maximal tissue displacement (at the end of the loading phase) was 11.1±1.2 nN, and fell to 5.0±0.45 nN by the end of the holding phase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c

claim: The force at the end of the holding phase was 5.0±0.45 nN.
source: The average force measured at maximal tissue displacement (at the end of the loading phase) was 11.1±1.2 nN, and fell to 5.0±0.45 nN by the end of the holding phase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c

claim: Most of the cell edges remain in a constant position during the holding phase.
source: During the holding phase, most of the cell edges remain in a constant position, although the green cantilever trace and a few nearby cell edges move slightly upward (Figure 2a and c'').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and c''

claim: The tissue must have been largely in mechanical equilibrium at the time the cantilever stopped moving.
source: Since most motion ceases as soon as the cantilever stops moving, the tissue must have been largely in mechanical equilibrium at the time the cantilever stopped moving; in other words, most of the tissue was deforming adiabatically during the loading phase.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that motion ceases when cantilever stops

claim: Most of the tissue was deforming adiabatically during the loading phase.
source: Since most motion ceases as soon as the cantilever stops moving, the tissue must have been largely in mechanical equilibrium at the time the cantilever stopped moving; in other words, most of the tissue was deforming adiabatically during the loading phase.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that tissue was in mechanical equilibrium

claim: The tissue is deforming without significant input from external friction during the loading phase.
source: This indicates that the tissue is deforming without significant input from external friction, which is consistent with the tissue deforming adiabatically (Figure 2d).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that β=0 in the deformation profiles

claim: During ventral furrow formation, the leading edge of the ectoderm travels toward the midline at a rate of approximately 0.1 µm/s.
source: During ventral furrow formation, the leading edge of the ectoderm travels toward the midline at a rate of approximately 0.1 µm/s (He et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Dissipative forces such as friction must be lower during ventral furrow formation than in the cantilever pulling experiments.
source: Since this is slower than the deformation rate in our experiments, dissipative forces such as friction must also be lower during ventral furrow formation.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of deformation rates

claim: Tissue deformation is largely adiabatic during ventral furrow formation.
source: Therefore, we can conclude that tissue deformation is also largely adiabatic during this morphogenetic process.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that friction is lower during ventral furrow formation

claim: During the loading phase, the applied force increases linearly with displacement, rather than with the rate of displacement.
source: During the loading phase (in which constant displacement is imposed), the applied force increases linearly with displacement, rather than with the rate of displacement (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c

claim: If viscous forces were dominant then the force should be proportional to the rate of displacement.
source: If viscous forces were dominant then the force should be proportional to the rate of displacement, which is not the case.
evidence: Based on established principles of fluid mechanics

claim: During the unloading phase, after the cantilever has been withdrawn, the tissue relaxes largely, though not entirely, back to its initial configuration.
source: During the unloading phase, after the cantilever has been withdrawn, the tissue relaxes largely, though not entirely, back to its initial configuration (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a

claim: The tissue itself is either an elastic or viscoelastic material.
source: These observations are both clearly consistent with the tissue itself being either an elastic or viscoelastic material.
evidence: Inferred from the observations of force-displacement relationship and tissue relaxation

claim: Elastic forces dominate over friction and viscous shear forces in this system during the loading phase.
source: The arguments given in the previous section for adiabatic deformation also mean that elastic forces dominate over friction and viscous shear forces in this system during the loading phase.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of adiabatic deformation

claim: The observation that force on the cantilever drops by only about half during the holding phase suggests that boundary constraints may be important.
source: The observation that force on the cantilever drops by only about half (not to zero) during the holding phase suggests that boundary constraints may be important.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of force dynamics during holding phase

claim: The cells are represented as open prisms with lateral and apical surfaces modeled as networks of elastic springs in the computational model.
source: The cells are represented as open prisms with lateral and apical surfaces modeled as networks of elastic springs (each with spring constant k); the basal surfaces are left open (Figure 4a'').
evidence: Description of the computational model

claim: The cytoplasm filling the cell interiors and the yolk are modeled as a Newtonian fluid, with viscosity set to 1000 cP.
source: The cytoplasm filling the cell interiors and the yolk are modeled as a Newtonian fluid, with viscosity set to the experimentally measured value of 1000 cP (Doubrovinski et al., 2017; Selvaggi et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on experimentally measured values from cited publications

claim: The perivitelline fluid is approximated by a Newtonian fluid with the viscosity of water (~1 cP).
source: the perivitelline fluid between the vitelline membrane and the cellular layer is approximated by a Newtonian fluid with the viscosity of water (~1 cP) (Figure 4b).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of water viscosity

claim: For a triangular network of springs approximation, the Poisson's ratio is 1/3.
source: Note that for this type of approximation, the Poisson's ratio is 1/3.
evidence: Based on established principles of material mechanics for triangular networks

claim: A value of k=0.001 nN/μm resulted in a curve that matched the experimental relaxation data extremely well.
source: Carrying out this parameter sweep, we found that a value of k=0.001 nN/μm (or equivalently E=0.0012) resulted in a curve that matched the data extremely well (Figure 5a and c, Simulation 1).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5

claim: For k=0.001 nN/μm, the predicted maximal force at the end of the loading phase was less than 0.2 nN.
source: However, for the value of k which best matched the decay dynamics (k=0.001 nN/μm, Simulation 1), the predicted maximal force at the end of the loading phase was less than 0.2 nN (Figure 5b and c, Simulation 1).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5

claim: The predicted maximal force of less than 0.2 nN is an order of magnitude lower than the forces measured directly from the deflection of calibrated cantilevers at the end of either the loading (~11 nN) or holding (~5 nN) phase.
source: This value is an order of magnitude lower than the forces measured directly from the deflection of our calibrated cantilevers at the end of either the loading (~11 nN) or holding (~5 nN) phase.
evidence: Comparison of computational predictions with experimental measurements

claim: For a given spring constant, the force required to deform the triangular network was greater than the force required to deform the hexagonal network by the same amount.
source: For a given spring constant, the force required to deform the triangular network was greater than the force required to deform the hexagonal network by the same amount (Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6a

claim: In the hexagonal-mesh case, the tissue relaxed back to its initial position more slowly as k increased.
source: In the hexagonal-mesh case, however, the tissue relaxed back to its initial position more slowly as k increased (Figure 6b).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6b

claim: The extent of tissue relaxation in the hexagonal-mesh case was lower as k increased.
source: Furthermore, the extent of tissue relaxation was also lower (Figure 6b and d).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6b and d

claim: The response of hexagonal and floppy networks during unloading is qualitatively different from triangular networks.
source: These results indicate that the response of hexagonal and floppy networks during unloading is qualitatively different.
evidence: Inferred from the computational modeling results

claim: The apical surface appears most similar to a stiff elastic sheet.
source: The apical surface appears most similar to a stiff elastic sheet, while the lateral surfaces and basal edges form a semi-hexagonal, and therefore floppy, network.
evidence: Based on the topology of cellular structures

claim: The lateral surfaces and basal edges form a semi-hexagonal, and therefore floppy, network.
source: The apical surface appears most similar to a stiff elastic sheet, while the lateral surfaces and basal edges form a semi-hexagonal, and therefore floppy, network.
evidence: Based on the topology of cellular structures

claim: In ferrofluid experiments with droplets that contact the basal edge, the speed of deformation decreased as the droplet approached the magnet.
source: In these previous experiments (reproduced in Figure 7a–a'), the speed of deformation decreased as the droplet approached the magnet, which we attributed to a build-up of elastic stress in the epithelium.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a-a'

claim: In ferrofluid experiments with smaller droplets positioned entirely inside the cell, the speed of deformation was constant or even increasing as the droplet approached the magnet.
source: In these experiments, the speed of deformation was constant or even increasing as the droplet approached the magnet, demonstrating that elastic stresses in this case were very small compared to the pulling force (Figure 7b').
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b'

claim: The difference in dynamics between large and small ferrofluid droplets demonstrates that the apical and lateral portions of the cell are softer than the basal edges.
source: This difference in dynamics demonstrates that the apical and lateral portions of the cell are softer, that is have a lower elastic modulus, than the basal edges.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ferrofluid experiments with different droplet sizes

claim: Increasing klateral and kbasal 20- to 30-fold resulted in much higher values for maximal force Fmax (going from 0.2 nN to nearly 7 nN), but resulted in very similar values for the decay constant τ (~50 s).
source: Increasing klateral and kbasal 20- to 30-fold resulted in much higher values for maximal force Fmax (going from 0.2 nN to nearly 7 nN), but resulted in very similar values for the decay constant τ (~50 s).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7c-c''

claim: Increased elasticity within floppy structural components primarily affects mechanics during loading (characterized by Fmax), with only minor effects on unloading (characterized by τ).
source: This validated our hypothesis that increased elasticity within floppy structural components should primarily affect mechanics during loading (characterized by Fmax), with only minor effects on unloading (characterized by τ).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: When kbasal and klateral were kept approximately constant, but kapical was increased about sixfold, this resulted in a dramatic change of decay constant τ, from 39 s to 9 s.
source: In contrast, when kbasal and klateral were kept approximately constant, but kapical was increased about sixfold, this resulted in a dramatic change of decay constant τ, from 39 s to 9 s (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: One parameter set (kapical = 0.007, klateral = 0.126, kbasal = 6.825) resulted in a maximal force (7 nN) that fell within the 5 nN to 11 nN range of maximal force measured directly from cantilever deflection in experiments.
source: Notably, one of the parameter sets used in our simulations (kapical = 0.007, klateral = 0.126, kbasal = 6.825) resulted in a maximal force (7 nN) that fell within the 5 nN to 11 nN range of maximal force measured directly from cantilever deflection in experiments.
evidence: Comparison of computational predictions with experimental measurements

claim: Assuming that basal domains are much stiffer than the apical and the lateral domains suffices to reconcile the model with measurement data.
source: To summarize, assuming that basal domains are much stiffer than the apical and the lateral domains suffices to reconcile the model with our measurement data.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental data

claim: Even at short pulling times, cells throughout the model embryo move from their initial positions, even on the opposite side of the embryo from the force application.
source: Plotting the displacement of cells in our model reveals that this explanation is not true. Even at short pulling times, cells throughout the model embryo move from their initial positions, even on the opposite side of the embryo from the force application, and even at the distant anterior and posterior poles (Figure 8a–a', Video 3).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8a-a' and Video 3

claim: When concentrated force was applied to one side of the embryo using a ferrofluid droplet, cells on the opposite side of the embryo clearly moved as well.
source: We next examined previously acquired experimental data (Doubrovinski et al., 2017) to see if the same might be true in vivo. Indeed, when concentrated force was applied to one side of the embryo using a ferrofluid droplet, cells on the opposite side of the embryo clearly moved as well (Figure 8b–b', Video 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8b-b' and Video 4

claim: Simulations reveal an upregulation of stress near the poles.
source: In fact, our simulations reveal an upregulation of stress near the poles (Figure 8c).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8c

claim: Geometrical constraints preventing free rotation of the tissue allow for the build-up of elastic stress throughout the tissue when force is applied locally.
source: In summary, geometrical constraints preventing free rotation of the tissue allow for the build-up of elastic stress throughout the tissue when force is applied locally.
evidence: Inferred from computational modeling and experimental observations

claim: Epithelial deformation is adiabatic during the loading phase of pulling experiments.
source: During the loading phase of our pulling experiments, we found that epithelial deformation is adiabatic and that mechanics are dominated by elastic forces and geometric constraints.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and analysis

claim: Mechanics during the loading phase are dominated by elastic forces and geometric constraints.
source: During the loading phase of our pulling experiments, we found that epithelial deformation is adiabatic and that mechanics are dominated by elastic forces and geometric constraints.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and analysis

claim: Deformations in the cantilever pulling experiments were comparable to (and even slightly faster than) the endogenous tissue deformation during ventral furrow formation.
source: Since deformations in our experiments were comparable to (and even slightly faster than) the endogenous tissue deformation during ventral furrow formation, these conclusions should apply to that process as well.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental deformation rates with published data on ventral furrow formation

claim: Experimental data could not be reconciled to a model in which the tissue was uniformly elastic along the apical-basal axis.
source: Surprisingly, our data could not be reconciled to a model in which the tissue was uniformly elastic along the apical-basal axis.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: Experimental data could be fit well by a model in which apical surfaces are significantly softer than basal surfaces.
source: In contrast, our data could be fit well by a model in which apical surfaces are significantly softer than basal surfaces.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: Experiments using small ferrofluid droplets showed that apical surfaces are significantly softer than basal surfaces.
source: Strikingly, experiments using small ferrofluid droplets also showed that apical surfaces are significantly softer than basal surfaces.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a-b

claim: The reason apical and basal structures contribute differently to force loading and unloading is because the apical structures are topologically stiff, while the basal (and lateral) structures are topologically floppy.
source: Using a simplified computational model, we demonstrated that the reason apical and basal structures contribute differently to force loading and unloading is because the apical structures are topologically stiff, while the basal (and lateral) structures are topologically floppy.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6

claim: Relaxation dynamics in general should be expected to primarily reveal elasticities of stiff (non-floppy) components.
source: Specifically, relaxation dynamics in general should be expected to primarily reveal elasticities of stiff (non-floppy) components.
evidence: Inferred from computational modeling results

claim: Geometrical constraints generate a significant force opposing tissue movement when force is applied locally within the Drosophila embryo.
source: Another unexpected result from this work is that geometrical constraints (which could alternatively be called system size effects because they depend on the system being 'small enough') generate a significant force opposing tissue movement when force is applied locally within the Drosophila embryo.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental data

claim: Any deformation, however small, propagates through the tissue on a time-scale of seconds.
source: As a result, any deformation, however small, propagates through the tissue on a time-scale of seconds.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental data

claim: D'Angelo et al. (2019) found an abrupt developmental change in mechanical response, with tissue deformation becoming much greater beginning about 16 min before the onset of gastrulation.
source: The authors carefully measured the response to a consistently applied magnetic force and found an abrupt developmental change in mechanical response, with tissue deformation becoming much greater beginning about 16 min before the onset of gastrulation.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: D'Angelo et al. (2019) proposed that a sudden softening of the epithelium and an abrupt increase in friction with the vitelline membrane could account for their observations.
source: Based on fitting these data to a computational model in which a 2D viscoelastic sheet moving over a substrate represented the epithelium and vitelline membrane, the authors proposed that a sudden softening of the epithelium and an abrupt increase in friction with the vitelline membrane could account for their observations.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: During the early stage of cellularization, cells are short and the 5 μm apically localized beads would be expected to be in mechanical contact with the very rigid basal side.
source: We note that during the early stage of cellularization, cells are short and the 5 μm apically localized beads would also be expected to be in mechanical contact with the very rigid basal side.
evidence: Inferred from cell dimensions and bead size

claim: At a later stage in cellularization, cells become taller and the bead should only contact the apical and/or the lateral cellular domains.
source: At a later stage in cellularization, cells become taller and the bead should only contact the apical and/or the lateral cellular domains, which we have demonstrated are much softer.
evidence: Inferred from cell dimensions and bead size, combined with experimental findings

claim: Previous studies of cellularization dynamics are consistent with the basal edge of the cells moving past the 5 μm magnetic beads at approximately 16 min before gastrulation.
source: Furthermore, previous studies of cellularization dynamics are consistent with the basal edge of the cells moving past the 5 μm magnetic beads at approximately 16 min before gastrulation (Figard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Differences in the apparent material properties reported in D'Angelo et al., 2019, reflect differences in the material properties of the cellular domains being probed, and not time-dependent mechanical changes of the entire epithelial layer due to developmental progression.
source: We therefore propose that differences in the apparent material properties reported in D'Angelo et al., 2019, reflect differences in the material properties of the cellular domains being probed, and not time-dependent mechanical changes of the entire epithelial layer due to developmental progression.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of experimental conditions and cell geometry

claim: Colcemid treatment blocks the apparent tissue softening observed by D'Angelo et al., 2019.
source: Importantly, our proposal also explains the observation that colcemid treatment blocks the apparent tissue softening (D'Angelo et al., 2019); microtubule depolymerization stops cellularization, so treated cells would remain short (Royou et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Previous data showed that tissue elasticity is overwhelmingly dominated by cortical F-actin.
source: Our previous data (Doubrovinski et al., 2017) showed that tissue elasticity is overwhelmingly dominated by cortical F-actin.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The basal side exhibits much stronger F-actin localization than either the apical or the lateral side.
source: At the same time, it is well established (Sokac and Wieschaus, 2008) that the basal side exhibits much stronger F-actin localization than either the apical or the lateral side.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The elastic modulus estimated from relaxation dynamics (E approximately = 0.001–0.01) provides a good estimate specifically of apical elasticity.
source: (1) The elastic modulus we estimated from relaxation dynamics (E approximately = 0.001–0.01) provides a good estimate specifically of apical elasticity.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental data

claim: Basal elasticity in this tissue is substantially higher than apical elasticity.
source: (2) Basal elasticity in this tissue is substantially higher than apical elasticity.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental data

claim: The fact that the force drops but then levels off during the holding phase implies that some elastic stress dissipates on the time-scale of a minute, but that some elastic stress persists on very long time-scales.
source: The fact that the force drops but then levels off during the holding phase implies two things: that some elastic stress dissipates on the time-scale of a minute, but that some elastic stress persists on very long time-scales.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of force dynamics during holding phase

claim: The tissue recoil is largely (85–100%) complete.
